label: copy-phase input token m
explanation: Fires whenever the token m is fed back as input during the copy phase (t > L), at every recall position and for any L, at about 46% of all m inputs overall. It is silent on every other input token. It is also essentially silent on m during the original phase (499 tiny activations around 0.02 of max, mostly at the last original positions). Magnitude is close to constant (median 3.48, max 3.79). The weakest activations (about 0.65-0.75 of max) occur when m is the first copied token, i.e. at recall_idx 1 right after <DEL>: this case makes up 73% of the bottom activation quartile and none of the upper three quartiles. The next output token, the previous token, and digit count have no appreciable effect.

issues: No systematic counterexample. On the test split there are 0 false positives. The 462 missed steps are tiny activations (about 0.01-0.07 of max) on original-phase m and hold 0.0% of activation mass. Test scores: P=1.0, R=0.995, F1=0.997, mass recall 0.9998.

The claim that the first copied token gives the weakest activations is confirmed. Restricting to recall_idx==1 covers 73.3% of the bottom quartile and 0% of the other three quartiles. Lowest-quartile examples all have m as the first token, at about 0.66-0.72 of max.

The original-phase claim is roughly accurate. There are 499 dev activations, concentrated at orig_idx 7-8 (344 of 499), but some occur at non-final positions (e.g. m at orig_idx 7 with L=9). 'Mostly at the last original positions' is slightly loose but not wrong.
Minor nuance: prev_tok 'l' shows up often in the very top activations (around 1.00 vs about 0.9 typical), so the previous token has a small effect on magnitude. This does not affect the predicate.
